historical_claims.anchor: Kazuo Ishiguro was born in Nagasaki in 1954 and moved with his family to England in 1960, when his father took up research work as an oceanographer.
historical_claims.source_locator: Ishiguro Nobel lecture: Nagasaki, move and father

historical_claims.anchor: In his Nobel lecture, Ishiguro described growing up with an imagined Japan sustained by family conversation, childhood memory, and materials sent from abroad.
historical_claims.source_locator: Nobel lecture 2017: preservation of an imagined Japan

historical_claims.anchor: Ishiguro and his wife Lorna arranged a four-week period in 1987 during which he cleared his schedule and wrote for much of each day.
Ishiguro had prepared through reading about servants, interwar politics, and the English countryside.
The book won the Booker Prize in 1989.
One of the novel's clearest moral tests concerns two Jewish employees, Ruth and Sarah.
historical_claims.source_locator: Novel episode; scholarly essay recounts Ruth and Sarah dismissals

description: Follows Stevens’s retrospective journey, examining service, dignity, political complicity, missed intimacy, and the language of self-excuse. Covers The road trip that requires an explanation; The writer and the making of the voice; A professional vocabulary that organizes a life; The life beneath the explanation.
